citation: Zarattini & Aziz (2023), Can Day Trading Really Be Profitable? Evidence of Sustainable Long-term Profits from Opening Range Breakout (ORB) Day Trading Strategy vs. Benchmark in the US Stock Market, SSRN Working Paper 4416622
journal_source: SSRN Working Paper (not journal-published as of our search)
asset: QQQ, SPY and a broader US equity universe (original paper)
signal: breakout above/below the first N-minute opening range of the regular session
target_variable: intraday directional continuation after the opening range
holding_period: intraday only, closed at session end (no overnight hold)
economic_explanation: Early-session order flow imbalance (overnight information being priced in at the open) tends to continue rather than mean-revert for a subset of sessions; a breakout of the initial range is used as a live signal of that imbalance
statistical_methodology: reported Sharpe ratios and benchmark comparison vs buy-and-hold in original paper (see source)
reported_t_stats_p_values: not independently re-verifiable -- see citation caveat below
reported_costs: modeled in original paper (see source); not independently re-verifiable here
reported_return: reported outperformance vs buy-and-hold benchmark in original paper
reported_sharpe: reported favourably vs benchmark in original paper
reported_drawdown: not independently re-verifiable -- see citation caveat below
replication_feasibility: medium -- mechanism (opening-range breakout, exit at session close) is simple and fully replicable; exact original parameters (range window, stop-loss rule) are NOT independently re-verifiable here
required_datasets: Intraday OHLCV bars covering each session's opening range through session close
suspected_look_ahead_risks: breakout must be confirmed on a bar CLOSE and acted on the following bar's open, never the breakout bar's own open/close, to avoid look-ahead -- enforced in our implementation
suspected_publication_bias_risks: SSRN working paper, not peer-reviewed; day-trading strategy papers carry a well-documented general risk of survivorship/backtest-overfitting bias in this literature segment
our_replication_result: Mechanism-only replication (not the original paper's exact parameters -- every host that would allow re-verification of those, SSRN included, was blocked by this session's network egress policy). Tested on MES/MGC/MCL x 15min/30min RTH-only bars (~21-67 sessions per cell) with three optional filters (momentum/gap-alignment, volume-confirmation, and an internal realized-volatility FEAR/GREED regime classifier) layered on individually. See reports/backtests/ORB_v1_MES_MGC_MCL_filters.json for the full 36-cell sweep.
our_robustness_result: No filter combination shows a robust edge once multiple-comparisons risk is accounted for. The single most extreme cell (MGC 30min, vol_regime=GREED: net +$2901, win rate 71%, naive t=2.67, n=28 trades) is the best result among 36 tested (instrument x bar_size x filter) cells -- under an uncorrected-multiple-testing null, seeing at least one |t|>2.67 among 36 independent draws has a non-trivial (roughly 40%) chance even with zero true edge, so this is far more consistent with a multiple-comparisons false positive than a real signal. No out-of-sample or held-out validation was performed on any of the 36 cells.
our_conclusion: The ORB mechanism itself (opening-range breakout, next-bar execution, session-close exit) is implemented and correctly enforces no-look-ahead. Across 36 (instrument x bar_size x filter) combinations, results are inconsistent in sign and magnitude both across instruments and within the same instrument across bar sizes, with no filter reliably improving on the unfiltered baseline. Sample sizes (roughly 7-67 trades per cell) are too small for any individual cell to be statistically meaningful, and testing 36 cells without a multiple-comparisons correction or a held-out validation split means the single best-looking cell should be treated as noise, not a finding. Additionally, all data tested is RTH-only (New York session); no London-open variant of this strategy has been tested. Overall: not a demonstrated edge.

citation: Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen (2012), Time Series Momentum, Journal of Financial Economics 104(2), 228-250
asset: 58 liquid futures and forward contracts across equity indices, currencies, commodities, and bonds
signal: sign of a single instrument's own trailing 12-month excess return
target_variable: next-month excess return of the same instrument
economic_explanation: Initial underreaction and delayed overreaction to information, plus trend-following/momentum trading by market participants, produce serial correlation in returns within each individual instrument (distinct from cross-sectional momentum, which ranks across instruments)
statistical_methodology: Time-series regression of each instrument's return on its own lagged sign; robustness checks across 1/3/6/12-month lookbacks reported to have consistent sign
reported_t_stats_p_values: reported significant t-stats in original paper (see source)
reported_costs: transaction costs discussed and found not to erode the effect materially in the original paper
reported_return: reported positive risk-adjusted returns across nearly all 58 instruments and multiple sub-periods in original paper
reported_sharpe: reported favourably (diversified portfolio Sharpe above 1 in original sample)
reported_drawdown: reported smaller crash risk than buy-and-hold in original paper (positive skew, gains in extreme-volatility periods)
in_sample_or_out_of_sample: in-sample (original paper's own sample), later extended out-of-sample by other authors
replication_feasibility: medium -- single-instrument time-series mechanism is directly testable with only MES/MGC/MCL (no cross-sectional universe needed, unlike Erb & Harvey P010); however this project's daily data depth (199-448 bars per instrument) cannot support the paper's own 12-month lookback with any usable sample, so only much shorter trading-day lookbacks (20/60/120) were tested
required_datasets: Each instrument's own historical price series only (no panel needed) -- available here
suspected_look_ahead_risks: signal computed from a bar's own close and only ever acted on at the following bar's open, enforced in our implementation
suspected_publication_bias_risks: widely cited and replicated paper; time-series momentum's live performance has been reported to have weakened since publication (2010s-2020s) in later practitioner and academic commentary, a relevant caveat for treating the original sample's Sharpe as current
our_replication_result: Tested as a majority-vote consensus across 20/60/120-trading-day lookbacks (not the paper's own single 12-month lookback, which our daily data depth cannot support) on MES/MGC/MCL daily bars. Net POSITIVE in raw dollar terms for all three instruments (base scenario: MES +$3406, MGC +$7343, MCL +$646). See reports/backtests/MULTI_HORIZON_TREND_v1_MES_MGC_MCL.json.
our_robustness_result: In every instrument the strategy badly underperforms a naive buy-and-hold benchmark over the identical window (MES captured 84% of buy-and-hold, MGC 49%, MCL only 16%) because all three instruments happened to trend strongly upward over their available sample windows and the strategy's occasional flat/short periods cost more than they saved. Trade counts are tiny (3, 20, 3 trades) and naive_t_stat is well under 1.0 for all three -- far from any meaningful significance.
our_conclusion: The consensus-voting fix for H002 (DUAL_MA_XOVER_v1)'s single-pair fragility works as intended -- it trades much less often and avoids obvious whipsaw losses -- but trading less often also means capturing less of a persistent trend, which is exactly what happened in this bull-biased sample. Result is observationally similar to H003's failure mode: nominally positive P&L that is mostly explained by the sample period's own directional drift, not a demonstrated timing edge.

citation: Barroso & Santa-Clara (2015), Momentum has its moments, Journal of Financial Economics 116(1), 111-120
signal: cross-sectional equity momentum, position sized inversely to trailing realized volatility of the momentum strategy's own returns
target_variable: risk-adjusted (Sharpe) momentum return, specifically crash risk reduction
economic_explanation: Momentum crashes cluster in a small number of high-volatility periods (often market rebounds after a crash); scaling exposure down when recent realized volatility is high avoids most of that crash risk while giving up relatively little of the calm-period return
statistical_methodology: Compares raw momentum portfolio Sharpe/skew to a volatility-managed version using an ex-ante realized-vol scalar
reported_t_stats_p_values: reported significant improvement in Sharpe ratio in original paper (see source)
reported_costs: not the paper's primary focus; discussed qualitatively
reported_return: reported similar mean return to unscaled momentum with much smaller left tail / crash risk
reported_sharpe: reported roughly double the unscaled momentum portfolio's Sharpe ratio in original paper
reported_drawdown: reported substantially reduced tail risk / crash magnitude versus unscaled momentum
replication_feasibility: medium -- the vol-scaling MECHANISM (size inversely to trailing realized vol) is directly applicable to any signal, including a single-instrument time-series trend signal; the paper's own cross-sectional equity-momentum setting is not replicable here with only 3 futures
required_datasets: The strategy's own trailing return series (available for any instrument/signal combination in this project)
suspected_look_ahead_risks: vol-scaling weight computed only from data available at the same close the trend signal is computed from, applied to the following day's return only -- enforced in our implementation
suspected_publication_bias_risks: widely cited paper; vol-managed strategies more broadly have been reported in later literature to sometimes underperform naive versions in strongly trending, low-reversal regimes (the scaling gives up upside in exactly the periods it also would have protected downside) -- directly relevant to what this project's own test found (see H006/H007)
our_replication_result: Applied the vol-scaling MECHANISM (not the paper's own cross-sectional equity-momentum setting) on top of H005's multi-horizon trend consensus signal for MES/MGC/MCL daily bars, as a continuously-rebalanced daily-mark-to-market position rather than H005's discrete stop-and-reverse trades. Net POSITIVE in raw dollar terms for all 3 instruments but WORSE relative to buy-and-hold than the unscaled H005 version in 2 of 3 instruments (MES 48% vs H005's 84% of benchmark; MGC 31% vs H005's 49%; MCL 17% vs H005's 16%, roughly unchanged). See reports/backtests/VOL_SCALED_TREND_v1_and_PORTFOLIO.json.
our_robustness_result: Vol-scaling capped exposure during high-volatility periods, but in this sample those periods often coincided with the strongest parts of the underlying rally -- exactly the mechanism Barroso & Santa-Clara's own caveat literature warns about (scaling down in high-vol periods that turn out to be the best-returning ones). A 3-asset portfolio combination of the vol-scaled signals (H007) showed a genuine, real diversification benefit in RISK terms (daily P&L stdev reduced by a factor of ~2.1x versus the naive sum of individual stdevs, consistent with the pairwise correlations all being negative or near-zero: -0.43, -0.23, -0.04) -- but the portfolio's overlapping 78-day window return was net NEGATIVE (-$2140) while a naive buy-and-hold of the same 3 instruments over the identical window was net positive (+$176). Diversification reduced risk exactly as theory predicts; it did not create a return edge that wasn't there to begin with.
our_conclusion: The vol-scaling mechanism works exactly as this literature describes -- it measurably reduces risk (both single-instrument drawdown and, combined across instruments, portfolio-level volatility via genuine diversification) -- but risk-scaling a signal that has no demonstrated directional edge (per H005) does not create one. Confirms the general principle (vol-scaling and diversification both do what they claim) while showing neither rescues an underlying signal that isn't there.

citation: Lou, Polk & Skouras (2019), A Tug of War: Overnight versus Intraday Expected Returns, Journal of Financial Economics 134(1), 192-213
asset: US equity indices and characteristic-sorted portfolios (original)
sampling_frequency: daily, decomposed into close-to-open and open-to-close legs
signal: none (descriptive decomposition, not a predictive signal) -- splits each day's return into overnight (close-to-open) and intraday (open-to-close) components
target_variable: which leg of the daily return structurally dominates the other over time
holding_period: overnight leg: close-to-open; intraday leg: open-to-close
economic_explanation: Overnight returns compensate informed/institutional investors for bearing risk while markets are closed (illiquidity/risk premium); intraday returns are more contaminated by uninformed retail order flow and short-term reversal, netting close to zero or negative over long samples in the paper's own equity sample
statistical_methodology: Compares cumulative overnight-only vs intraday-only portfolio returns over the sample
reported_t_stats_p_values: reported significant divergence between the two legs in original paper (see source)
reported_costs: not the paper's primary focus for the core decomposition result
reported_return: reported overnight leg substantially outperforming intraday leg in original US equity sample
reported_sharpe: not the primary reported metric in the original paper's core result
replication_feasibility: high -- the decomposition needs only each bar's own open/close, directly computable from daily OHLCV data already on disk for all 3 instruments
suspected_look_ahead_risks: each leg's return is only knowable once it completes (open known at open, close known at close); the backtest engine only ever acts on a leg's own already-known open/close pair, no look-ahead
suspected_publication_bias_risks: widely cited; original finding is specific to US equities during specific decades -- applying the same structural question to a stock index FUTURE, a metal, and an energy future is a genuinely different test, not an assumption that the equity finding transfers
our_replication_result: MCL (crude oil): intraday leg strongly positive and consistent in BOTH halves of the sample when split chronologically (first half net +$1357 t=1.91, second half net +$1903 t=1.66) -- the most robust result of this entire session. MGC (gold): overnight leg positive in both halves but decaying sharply (first half net +$15,780 t=2.72, second half net +$5,808 t=0.52) -- directionally consistent, magnitude not stable. MES (equity index): both legs weak, overnight leg captures only 42% of buy-and-hold, intraday only 3%, no strong finding either direction. See reports/backtests/SESSION_DECOMP_v1_MES_MGC_MCL.json.
our_robustness_result: MCL intraday leg survives a chronological split-sample check (both halves independently positive with similar t-stats and magnitude) and survives the stress cost scenario (net degrades from $3260 to $2464, about 24%, still strongly positive). MGC overnight leg also survives stress costs well (net degrades only ~9%, from $20,156 to $18,368) but the split-sample check shows its apparent edge concentrated in the first half of the sample -- treat as directionally suggestive, not confirmed.
our_conclusion: The strongest, most differentiated finding of this project to date: crude oil's (MCL) daily return is structurally concentrated in the REGULAR TRADING SESSION (intraday), not overnight -- the opposite pattern from the classic equity anomaly this paper documents, and opposite to what MES itself shows (weakly overnight-favoring, like equities). This makes some economic sense (EIA inventory reports, OPEC news, and US macro data all land during NY trading hours for crude, unlike equities' classic overnight risk-premium story) but was not assumed going in -- it was found empirically. Gold's overnight-dominance is suggestive but not confirmed by the split-sample check. Not yet a tradeable edge (needs HAC-adjusted significance testing, longer history, and true out-of-sample validation before being trusted with capital) but the first result in this project's hypothesis ledger that clears a meaningfully higher bar than every prior rejected hypothesis.
status: mixed (MCL intraday leg: provisional pass, pending further robustness testing; MGC overnight leg: inconclusive; MES: failed)

reported_sharpe: reported favourably versus the market in original paper
in_sample_or_out_of_sample: in-sample (original paper's own sample), later shown by other authors to have decayed post-publication
replication_feasibility: medium -- the general MECHANISM (hedged spread, z-score entry/exit) is directly applicable to a single commodity's front/next term structure; the paper's own setting (matched pairs across many equities) cannot be replicated with only 3 futures in 3 different asset classes
required_datasets: Front and next contract daily prices for the same commodity (only available for MCL in this project -- MES/MGC next-contract history was inspected during the depth assessment but never persisted to disk)
suspected_look_ahead_risks: z-score computed only from data through the current bar's own close, acted on only at the following bar's open -- enforced in our implementation
suspected_publication_bias_risks: widely cited; pairs-trading returns have been reported in later literature to have decayed substantially since the strategy became well-known and crowded -- a real caveat for treating the original sample's results as current
our_replication_result: Applied to MCL front/next (MCLV6/MCLX6) daily spread, lookback=20, entry_z=1.5, exit_z=0.25 (fixed ex-ante, not fit to data). Only 10 trades over 199 days (7 short-spread, 3 long-spread). Net NEGATIVE in all 3 cost scenarios (base -$313, conservative -$343, stress -$393), win rate 30%, naive t-stat -0.95. See reports/backtests/SPREAD_MEAN_REV_v1_MCL.json.
our_robustness_result: n=10 trades is far too small to draw any conclusion, positive or negative -- this is the smallest sample of any hypothesis tested this session. Unlike H003 (ROLL_YIELD_CARRY_v1), this result is NOT contaminated by outright market beta (the position is hedged front-vs-next by construction), so the negative result is at least a clean, uncontaminated negative -- not an artifact of an unhedged directional bet.
our_conclusion: No edge found, but also no ambiguity about why: MCL's front/next spread simply did not move far enough, often enough, from its own 20-day trailing mean to generate a meaningful sample in this ~9-month window. This is a genuine data-availability limitation (longer history would be needed for a fair test of whether commodity term-structure spreads mean-revert in a tradeable way) rather than a demonstrated absence of the effect.
